title: Fatal primary amoebic meningoencephalitis in a Norwegian tourist returning from Thailand
case_prompt:
A 71-year-old woman was admitted to a local hospital in Oslo hours after returning from a four-week holiday in Thailand. She had a two-day history of fatigue and developed rapid onset of nausea, vomiting, fever, and exhaustion. On examination, she was febrile (39.5 °C) with a respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 12×10^9 cells/L and a C-reactive protein level of 9 mg/L. Intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin were started for presumed urosepsis, but later that day she became confused, developed speech disturbances, and was noted to have nuchal rigidity.

She was transferred to the tertiary care center and received 4 g of ceftriaxone. On arrival, she had obvious nuchal rigidity, incoherent speech, motor agitation, and confusion. Her Glasgow Coma Scale score was initially 12, dropping to 9, at which point she was intubated. A cerebral CT scan with angiography showed no acute ischemia, hemorrhage, or vascular occlusion. 

A lumbar puncture yielded cloudy cerebrospinal fluid under increased pressure. CSF analysis revealed a glucose concentration of 0.1 mmol/L (serum glucose 11.1 mmol/L), a protein level of 6.9 g/L, and 2115 leukocytes/mm^3 with 87.3% neutrophils. An acridine orange stain of the CSF showed no microbes. A nigrosin stain did not reveal cryptococci, although the examiner noted the presence of unidentified elements.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial meningitis was considered because of fever, nuchal rigidity, and neutrophilic pleocytosis — “bacterial meningitis now appeared likely.”  
2. Urosepsis was the initial diagnosis owing to fever and leukocytosis — “on suspicion of urosepsis… therapy commenced… but the patient’s condition rapidly deteriorated…”  
3. Resistant bacterial infection was considered given recent travel to an endemic region — “infection was presumably acquired in a region endemic for highly resistant bacteria,” prompting meropenem and vancomycin.  
4. Cryptococcal meningitis was suspected after failure to identify bacteria and lack of response to antibiotics — “due to the absence of an identified cause and lack of response to antibiotics, cryptococcal meningitis was suspected,” yet nigrosin stain was negative for cryptococci.  
5. Viral meningitis was investigated but ruled out by negative PCR assays — “PCR assays for possible bacterial or viral causes… were negative.”  
6. Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis was suspected based on incidental low‐identity match to Naegleria on fungal PCR, travel history, and absence of other pathogens — “This finding prompted a suspicion of primary amoebic meningoencephalitis, taking into account the clinical presentation, travel history, and lack of any other identified microbial agent.”
